author: xhigh4
claim: For the target hypotheses, the explicit vector w=(I-Q)^{-1}u is nonzero and satisfies HQw=w.
evidence: Since Q has no nonzero fixed vector, ker(I-Q)={0}; in finite dimension, A:=I-Q is invertible. Orthogonality gives I-Q^T=-Q^T(I-Q), so A^{-T}=-(I-Q)^{-1}Q. Because (I-Q)^{-1} commutes with Q and (I-Q)^{-1}Q=(I-Q)^{-1}-I, we obtain A^{-T}=I-A^{-1}. Thus, from u^T u=1, 2u^T A^{-1}u=u^T(A^{-1}+A^{-T})u=1. With w=A^{-1}u, Qw=w-u, so u^TQw=1/2-1=-1/2. Hence (I-HQ)w=(I-Q)w+2uu^TQw=u-u=0. Also w is nonzero because A is invertible and u is nonzero. author: high
claim: If A is a real n by n orthogonal matrix with no nonzero fixed vector, then det(A)=(-1)^n. Consequently, for H=I-2uu^T and Q as in the problem, det(HQ)=(-1)^(n+1), so HQ must have a nonzero fixed vector.
evidence: Over C, every eigenvalue lambda of a real orthogonal matrix A has |lambda|=1: if Az=lambda z, then ||Az||^2=z^*A^T A z=||z||^2, hence |lambda|=1. Nonreal eigenvalues occur with the same algebraic multiplicity as their conjugates, and each conjugate pair has product 1. The only real eigenvalues are 1 and -1. Absence of a nonzero real fixed vector excludes eigenvalue 1 (a complex fixed vector would have a nonzero real or imaginary part fixed). Thus the spectrum consists of r copies of -1 and conjugate pairs, so n-r is even and det(A)=(-1)^r=(-1)^n. Meanwhile H acts by -1 on span(u) and by 1 on u-perp, hence det(H)=-1; therefore det(HQ)=(-1)det(Q)=(-1)^(n+1). If HQ had no fixed vector, the same determinant rule would give det(HQ)=(-1)^n, a contradiction.

glossary.r: the algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalue -1

author: high2
claim: If Q is a real orthogonal matrix with no nonzero fixed vector and A=(Q-I)^{-1}, then A+A^{\mathsf T}=-I. Consequently, for every unit vector u, u^{\mathsf T}Au=-1/2.
evidence: The fixed-vector hypothesis gives ker(Q-I)={0}, hence Q-I is invertible. Orthogonality gives Q^{\mathsf T}=Q^{-1}. Therefore A^{\mathsf T}=(Q^{-1}-I)^{-1}=(-Q^{-1}(Q-I))^{-1}=-AQ. From A(Q-I)=I one gets AQ=I+A, so A^{\mathsf T}=-I-A. Thus A+A^{\mathsf T}=-I. Since the scalar u^{\mathsf T}Au equals its transpose u^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}u, twice this scalar is u^{\mathsf T}(A+A^{\mathsf T})u=-u^{\mathsf T}u=-1.

links.statement: If Q is a real orthogonal matrix with no nonzero fixed vector and A=(Q-I)^{-1}, then A+A^{\mathsf T}=-I and u^{\mathsf T}Au=-1/2 for every real unit vector u.

author: xhigh3
claim: The vector x=(I-Q)^{-1}u is a nonzero fixed vector of HQ.
evidence: Because Q has no nonzero fixed vector, ker(I-Q)={0}; in finite dimension I-Q is invertible, so x=(I-Q)^{-1}u is defined. Since u^T u=1, u is nonzero, and hence x is nonzero. The defining equation is u=(I-Q)x=x-Qx. Orthogonality of Q gives ||Qx||^2=||x||^2, so 1=||u||^2=||x-Qx||^2=2||x||^2-2x^TQx. Thus u^T x=(x-Qx)^T x=||x||^2-x^TQx=1/2. Also Qx=x-u, hence u^TQx=u^Tx-u^Tu=1/2-1=-1/2. Therefore HQx=(I-2uu^T)Qx=Qx-2u(u^TQx)=Qx+u=x.

author: high3
claim: For the given real orthogonal Q with no nonzero fixed vector and the reflection H=I-2uu^{\mathsf T}, one has det(Q)=(-1)^n and det(HQ)=(-1)^{n+1}; consequently HQ has eigenvalue 1 and hence a nonzero real fixed vector.
evidence: Immediate-conclusions record: {"statement":"The determinant parity forces a fixed vector for HQ.","justification_type":"calculation","confidence":0.99,"is_fragile":false,"fragility_reason":"","suggested_followup":"none","scope":"global"}. Proof: Every complex eigenvalue of a real orthogonal matrix has modulus 1; nonreal eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs whose products are 1, and every real eigenvalue is ±1. Since Q has no eigenvalue 1, its real eigenvalues are all -1. If their algebraic multiplicity is r, then n-r is even and det(Q)=(-1)^r=(-1)^n. The map H sends u to -u and fixes u^\perp, so det(H)=-1 and det(HQ)=(-1)^{n+1}. If HQ had no eigenvalue 1, applying the same parity argument to the orthogonal matrix HQ would give det(HQ)=(-1)^n, a contradiction. Since HQ-I is a singular real matrix, its real kernel contains a nonzero vector.

author: xhigh
claim: Under the hypotheses of the problem, the unique vector w satisfying (I-Q)w=u is nonzero and satisfies HQw=w.
evidence: If (I-Q)y=0, then Qy=y; the hypothesis therefore gives y=0. Thus I-Q is injective, and since it is a linear endomorphism of the finite-dimensional space R^n, it is surjective. Hence there is a unique w with (I-Q)w=u. The equality u^T u=1 implies u is nonzero, so w is nonzero. From (I-Q)w=u we have Qw=w-u. Since Q is orthogonal, w^T w=(Qw)^T(Qw)=(w-u)^T(w-u)=w^T w-2u^T w+u^T u, so u^T w=1/2. Hence u^T Qw=u^T(w-u)=-1/2, and HQw=(I-2uu^T)Qw=Qw-2u(u^TQw)=(w-u)+u=w.
